title: Projecting Roles: Minutes, Usage and Team Context
markdown:
<sub>Proposed by the synthesis, not on the user's list.</sub>

**Summary.** Project minutes first, then role, then usage and opportunity, then production, and put narrative and hype last. Every team has 240 minutes and one ball per game, so add up your projections for each roster and scale them back before the 2026-10-18 auction. Coach habits, rotation depth and positional crowding decide who actually gets those minutes. Use them to find value and to spot players to fade.

## The order of evidence

Rank your evidence in this order: minutes, then role, then usage and opportunity, then production. Narrative and hype come last. A second version of the order runs minutes per game, then usage and role, then shot diet, then category production, then efficiency, with games played last. Both versions start with minutes and put the story around a player at the bottom. ([09-01](https://youtu.be/skKXe2CRl8Q?t=336), [08-09](https://youtu.be/8d--aL_xxwE?t=1618))

Usage and minutes are the two stats most closely tied to fantasy value. They are also stable from year to year: 0.83 for usage and 0.78 for minutes per game. So a real breakout usually needs a role change. Look for an injury, a trade or a free agency departure that frees up shots. If you see a player's minutes or usage differently from the consensus, move him on your auction sheet to match. Do not just copy the ranking. ([08-26](https://youtu.be/sTtFUy7IoJI?t=100), [08-09](https://youtu.be/8d--aL_xxwE?t=534), [09-10](https://youtu.be/W-R1dzem32s?t=531), [09-09](https://youtu.be/7BllEsdNLoM?t=420))

Judge last season's rank in context: role, teammates, injuries and minutes. Base value on the player's current situation, not on how much you like him. A per-game rank earned in limited minutes suggests upside if his minutes grow. That is a good profile for the last nominations of the auction, when most rosters are nearly full. ([10-04](https://youtu.be/tnzmsYUA4yQ?t=444), [09-17](https://youtu.be/DubdKKhMWHo?t=1528), [09-21](https://youtu.be/egRrai3Ax38?t=1036))

## The 240-minute check

Every NBA game has 240 minutes to split among about 10 players. Before the auction, write down a minutes projection for each team's rotation and add it up. If the total is well over 240, your projections are too high and someone has to lose minutes. Ask of every target: can he realistically get enough of those 240? ([09-10](https://youtu.be/W-R1dzem32s?t=1934), [10-01](https://youtu.be/aLP080hxizA?t=1594))

Use these minutes tiers. Starters play about 29 to 35 minutes. Bench players play 17 to 20. A '.5 starter' plays about 24 to 25. Simple math shows the limit. Five starters at 32 minutes use 160, which leaves 80 for the bench, about four players at 20 each. If your sheet has six or seven players from one team at 30 or more, cut someone. ([10-03](https://youtu.be/_O9pc_u5vH0?t=245), [09-10](https://youtu.be/W-R1dzem32s?t=1934))

Depth moves the numbers. On a team with poor depth, role players' minutes go up: 22 minutes can become 26, and 27 can become 31. Small differences matter. Losing even two to three minutes a game limits a player's upside and lowers his draft value. Per-minute big men only have fantasy value when they get enough minutes, so look for teams whose thin depth forces those minutes on them. ([08-22](https://youtu.be/LXZLrL90crE?t=953), [06-25](https://youtu.be/lOshTzDA4SA?t=1357), [06-30](https://youtu.be/4GDfg2n2l8o?t=1105))

## Usage: there is only one ball

Run the same check on usage. When several high-usage players end up on one team, last season's numbers cannot all hold. If you add up their past usage without regressing it, the team projection becomes unrealistic. Bring every player down. Comparing those scaled-back numbers with the market price is how you find value or players to fade. ([08-26](https://youtu.be/sTtFUy7IoJI?t=2255), [08-11](https://youtu.be/YJk7ZFKFqnI?t=1141), [08-11](https://youtu.be/YJk7ZFKFqnI?t=1155), [06-29](https://youtu.be/bHA-JoW3reE?t=1081))

When stars are added, a player's share of usage matters more than his raw usage. When a dominant player joins, the usage of everyone around him drops. The existing star loses usage and assist upside even if his minutes stay the same. A player losing about 25% of his usage cannot keep his fantasy output. The players who depend on usage to produce lose the most. The notes name Barrett and Quickley as examples. Players who do not depend on usage, like Barnes, are hurt less. Even if the new teammates miss games, they will play more than zero, so some loss is certain. ([07-13](https://youtu.be/Rqb5GdrSweY?t=936), [09-10](https://youtu.be/dlo7L8Ru91A?t=817), [08-26](https://youtu.be/sTtFUy7IoJI?t=1975), [06-30](https://youtu.be/JMSLg6yz-M0?t=283), [09-10](https://youtu.be/dlo7L8Ru91A?t=822), [07-02](https://youtu.be/P6TNP-g0wzY?t=580))

When stars leave, count the usage that goes out and the usage that comes in. If a team loses high-usage players and brings back fewer, the leftover usage creates targets. Expect bumps for the secondary options. A bench scorer may dip if he moves into a lower-priority role. A player who was third in line for the ball next to two stars can jump in value, especially in assists, once one star leaves. Check his splits from games when he played with only one of them. A star trade that returns several players and lottery picks does not open value for everyone. Use offensive load, which includes assists and potential assists, and not just usage when ball handlers leave. ([06-23](https://youtu.be/nnWX_ObljOE?t=413), [06-23](https://youtu.be/nnWX_ObljOE?t=382), [07-01](https://youtu.be/W3THnI7wWdA?t=855), [06-25](https://youtu.be/ya2VYRJ1BN0?t=1151), [07-01](https://youtu.be/W3THnI7wWdA?t=892), [06-23](https://youtu.be/9tb1ARBEmQU?t=295))

Think in our nine categories. A third offensive option needs big minutes and very efficient shooting to matter, and that is not a likely high-upside outcome. When a player's offensive usage rises, his blocks tend to drop, and less offensive load can bring them back. Balanced teams spread scoring and lower individual peaks compared with teams built around one player. Before you expect a role player to break out, check how many high-usage stars are on his roster. One trade example: Michael Porter Jr.'s value moves a lot depending on whether he is in Brooklyn or Denver. ([06-25](https://youtu.be/ya2VYRJ1BN0?t=479), [08-05](https://youtu.be/CI4k8ofUXXk?t=1502), [08-05](https://youtu.be/CI4k8ofUXXk?t=1012), [07-30](https://youtu.be/TiiaNZCJNs8?t=783), [06-25](https://youtu.be/lOshTzDA4SA?t=140))

## Coaches and rotation depth

A coach who plays heavy minutes, or who benches players for poor defense, can decide whether a player is a value or a bust. The notes name Ime Udoka and Nick Nurse as the coaches who lean on their starters the most. Under Rick Carlisle, expect low regular-season minutes for starters, especially starting centers. Bid up starters for heavy-minutes coaches. Trim starting centers under Carlisle. ([10-01](https://youtu.be/aLP080hxizA?t=199), [08-12](https://youtu.be/yoCTTlJ_tPQ?t=743), [08-10](https://youtu.be/sfCe7fS9daM?t=1146))

Very deep rotations with short stints spread minutes thin. That hurts fantasy value even if it helps the real team. A 12 to 13 player rotation caps everyone, even starters. No Pistons player got much past 35 minutes. Coaches do not play 12 or more players in a stable rotation. So on overstocked rosters, some rotation candidates get nothing until injuries open minutes. ([08-17](https://youtu.be/LcZcvk8s1xQ?t=1208), [08-12](https://youtu.be/p9XE5jFqhvs?t=1386), [07-27](https://youtu.be/0AptxcRW0RE?t=357))

Team goals shape minutes too. A team that needs to win will play its star more than a cautious, rebuilding team did. A coach fighting for his job may lean on veterans instead of developing young players. A coaching change can also change the style of play, which affects offensive rebounds, steals and pace. ([06-25](https://youtu.be/ya2VYRJ1BN0?t=437), [07-31](https://youtu.be/oEywzBZfAvY?t=2073), [08-14](https://youtu.be/owlM6b8oUd0?t=2123))

## Positional fit and crowded rosters

Our league drafts only 144 players, fewer than five per NBA team on average. When a team has too many players at the same positions, minutes get spread thin and fewer of them are draftable. Not every good player on a crowded position gets minutes. Project the whole rotation before you nominate or bid on anyone from that team. Look at full rosters before deciding where a player belongs on your sheet. ([07-02](https://youtu.be/P6TNP-g0wzY?t=2340), [08-14](https://youtu.be/owlM6b8oUd0?t=57), [06-29](https://youtu.be/bHA-JoW3reE?t=1062))

Lineup choices trickle down. Playing small cuts center minutes and opens wing minutes. Playing big squeezes the forwards. Position labels are semantics. Judge a guard by his on-ball usage and assist rate, not by the point guard title. In a one-for-one positional swap, the analysis is simple: the incoming player takes the outgoing player's usage, and teammates move up or down from there. ([09-29](https://youtu.be/XSPJL_mlFXo?t=259), [08-06](https://youtu.be/gTsfR5PxAMY?t=1585), [06-30](https://youtu.be/JMSLg6yz-M0?t=331))

On crowded rosters where minutes and usage swing from game to game, do not pay extra for reliability. Weekly H2H rewards steady production, and these players do not give it. Do not spend auction money on low-ceiling role players on bad, unsettled teams just because they might start. Teams usually try the option that protects ego, salary, draft pedigree or trade capital first. They only make harder rotation changes after that option clearly fails, so expect any fix to come in season, through waivers. ([08-11](https://youtu.be/YJk7ZFKFqnI?t=2040), [06-30](https://youtu.be/JMSLg6yz-M0?t=982), [08-23](https://youtu.be/hm5-fiCa5S4?t=734))

## Signals, disagreements and in-season use

The experts disagree on coach talk. One side says to be skeptical of what coaches say about minutes and roles. Some coaches have a track record of saying things that did not come true. The other side says that when a coach publicly talks up a player, you should treat it as a signal. A practical middle path: give the praise weight only when the 240-minute check and the depth chart support it, and discount it from coaches with a history of misleading. Ignore what players say about each other entirely. ([10-03](https://youtu.be/_O9pc_u5vH0?t=359), [08-12](https://youtu.be/p9XE5jFqhvs?t=1447), [07-27](https://youtu.be/0AptxcRW0RE?t=1713), [10-02](https://youtu.be/ZYllcj4o6_A?t=2782))

The experts also differ on how much a starting job matters. One note says starting usually means more minutes and helps value. Another says a starting spot can matter less than minutes, because a bench player can play about as many minutes as a nominal starter. Follow the minutes. When drafters fear that a player might lose his starting job, his price drops. If your minutes projection says he starts, that discount is value at the auction. Under a new coach, preseason starting lineups are weaker signals than under a coach whose habits you know, so do not overreact to them two days before the draft. ([09-25](https://youtu.be/Bi1cEM03k9Y?t=384), [08-04](https://youtu.be/_WjOjp6Qu8E?t=683), [09-21](https://youtu.be/egRrai3Ax38?t=822), [09-29](https://youtu.be/XSPJL_mlFXo?t=1819))

Other team signals help. A big contract or a strong extension shows trust and a role that could grow. A player who simply picks up his option may not be in the long-term plans. Use beat reporters as background for draft, trade and waiver decisions. With so much movement this year, every stage of the auction will be volatile, so bid with your rotation sheet in hand. ([07-01](https://youtu.be/W3THnI7wWdA?t=1265), [08-14](https://youtu.be/owlM6b8oUd0?t=756), [08-27](https://youtu.be/ZAyie8lKyYc?t=66), [07-13](https://youtu.be/Rqb5GdrSweY?t=546))

In season, injuries reset the math. When stars on a crowded team miss games, the others get more scoring chances. A player's baseline only recovers while those teammates are out. Injuries on a deep team can hand real minutes to fringe players, as they did in Dallas the last couple of years. On thin non-playoff teams, an injury to a main player turns weak depth into a problem for the players left. Injury risk also works both ways: injury-prone teammates miss games too, which can open usage for your player. Spend FAB on daily waivers when an injury opens minutes, within the 6 adds per week. Use trades to sell players whose usage bump depends on a teammate's absence before he returns, ahead of the 2027-03-04 deadline and the playoffs that end 2027-03-28. ([08-06](https://youtu.be/gTsfR5PxAMY?t=504), [06-29](https://youtu.be/bHA-JoW3reE?t=349), [07-27](https://youtu.be/0AptxcRW0RE?t=363), [08-18](https://youtu.be/FxaSnyk9g90?t=147), [07-14](https://youtu.be/xHRF06_E9HE?t=688))
